4.text:
There wasn't a single moment. It was more of a slow feeling that kept getting louder.

I spent eight years in hospitality. Front desk, then operations, then managing a team of twenty during the chaos of post-pandemic reopening. I was good at it. I genuinely loved parts of it.

But somewhere around 2022 I started noticing something. Every problem I actually enjoyed solving had nothing to do with room assignments or shift schedules. It was the systems underneath. Why is this process broken. How do we make this faster. Who is this actually serving.

I didn't wake up one day and decide to build a tech product. It was more like I kept following the thread that felt most alive, and one day I looked up and realized where I was standing.

I started learning Python in the mornings before my shift. Badly, at first. Very badly. I watched YouTube tutorials in hotel parking lots on my lunch break. I built small, stupid things that didn't work and then slowly worked.

JobMatch AI didn't come from a lightning bolt moment or a dramatic resignation. It came from about eighteen months of quiet accumulation. Small decisions. Uncomfortable learning. A lot of "I have no idea what I'm doing but I'm going to try anyway."

I think that's actually how most real transitions work. Not a leap. More like a slow walk toward something that keeps making sense.

5.text:
Most hotels are paying for tools they barely use.

I spent years in hotel operations watching this happen up close. A property management system with 200 features. Staff trained on maybe 15 of them. Contracts renewing automatically every year because nobody had the bandwidth to evaluate whether the software still made sense.

The waste was quiet and constant.

When I started building JobMatch AI, I kept thinking about that pattern. How much of what we buy in hospitality actually gets used versus what just sits there looking impressive in a vendor deck.

I talked to a mid-size hotel group last month that had consolidated three overlapping tools into one workflow they actually understood. Their ops team estimated 750 hours saved over the year. Not from buying something new. From stopping the bleed on what they already had.

No extra cost. Just clarity about what was working and the honesty to cut what was not.

Coming from hospitality into tech, I notice I am still thinking about the same problems. Resources are tight. Time is tighter. And the fanciest solution is rarely the right one.

Sometimes the most useful thing is just knowing what you already have.
